claim: The closest evidence is a slicing study that ran from 100 to 15,000 rows.
quote: To break this confound, this study employed a large-scale dataset slicing protocol (from N=100 to N=15,000 rows) alongside a matched-volume quality ablation.

claim: The Small-Sample Illusion study reports that models perform indistinguishably at small scales and that a distinct gradient-boosted tree advantage emerges as sample sizes increase.
quote: models perform indistinguishably at small scales. As sample sizes increase, a distinct gradient-boosted tree advantage emerges.

claim: The same abstract names a stabilisation point of 2,500 rows.
quote: Ultimately, this study overtly identifies exactly N=2,500 rows as the new empirical stabilisation point.

claim: Grinsztajn and colleagues report that tree-based models stay state-of-the-art at about 10K samples, even without counting their speed advantage.
quote: Results show that tree-based models remain state-of-the-art on medium-sized data ($\sim$10K samples) even without accounting for their superior speed.

claim: Grinsztajn and colleagues report that tree-based models are superior for every random search budget, and the performance gap stays wide even after a large number of random search iterations.
quote: tree-based models are superior for every random search budget, and the performance gap stays wide even after a large number of random search iteration.

claim: In Kadra and colleagues' study, regularization cocktails for MLPs were statistically significantly better than XGBoost after 30 minutes of HPO time.
quote: After 30 minutes of HPO time, regularization cocktails are statistically significantly better than XGBoost.

claim: Grinsztajn and colleagues caution that the datasets in that paper differ from theirs, including game-inspired deterministic ones where the method does very well.
quote: though the datasets considered in their paper are quite different, in particular with the presence of "deterministic" game-inspired datasets in Kadra et al. [2021b], on which their method performs very well and contributes markedly to the overall benchmark results.

claim: It has been conclusively proven that tabPFN is reported to clearly outperform boosted trees on datasets with up to 1,000 training points.
quote: On the 18 datasets in the OpenML-CC18 suite that contain up to 1 000 training data points, up to 100 purely numerical features without missing values, and up to 10 classes, we show that our method clearly outperforms boosted trees and performs on par with complex state-of-the-art AutoML systems with up to 230$\times$ speedup.

claim: TabPFN is reported to outperform all previous methods on datasets with up to 10,000 samples by a wide margin, using substantially less training time.
quote: outperforms all previous methods on datasets with up to 10,000 samples by a wide margin, using substantially less training time.

claim: One study on a CPU without GPU reports that tree ensembles trained in 0.1-0.2 seconds against 0.6-0.7 seconds for a DNN at n = 500.
quote: In the n = 500 simulation, tree ensembles train in 0.1-0.2 seconds while DNN training requires 0.6-0.7 seconds.

claim: The estimation study comparing tree ensembles and deep learning reports that deep neural networks achieve the minimal MSE when facing strong nonlinearity with moderate or large sample sizes.
quote: they achieve the minimal MSE when facing strong nonlinearity with moderate or large sample sizes.
